title: What’s your workflow for using AI to design game UI that feels like part of the game?
author: KamiYui_5555
selftext:
I’m working on a sci-fi game, and the UI I get from AI keeps looking like a generic web dashboard. I want the menus and transitions to feel like they belong to the same world as the game. It’s not enough for each screen to look good on its own if moving between them breaks immersion.

I can usually tell what feels off when I see it. The hard part is turning that into direction the AI can carry across screens. I can write out what’s wrong and go through several rounds of fixes, but I’m still a long way from a result I’d be happy to ship.

If you’ve found a workflow that works, what do you actually give the AI before it starts? Do you design one reference screen yourself, mock up a few connected screens, or give it assets and rules for layout, typography, and motion? And which decisions do you keep in your own hands?

I’d love to hear how you got from a first draft to something that held up across multiple screens in-game. A rough walkthrough of one real example would be more useful to me than a list of tools.

I really like how the title screen and party menu feel like part of the same game, even with such different layouts. 

Did you sketch each screen separately, or was one rough mockup enough to carry the style across?

replies.author: MotherVehkingMuatra
replies.body: One mockup was enough for me! It didn't implement the menu screen nicely at first but I got it to take another look and it nailed it after just two tries.

comments.author: pippinlitli
comments.body:
What helped me most was to stop describing each screen and write down the rules of the world's interface once, then reuse them for every screen.

1. A short style sheet in plain words: 2-3 colours with their role (one for danger, one for active), one font for headings and one for numbers, frame shape (sharp corners, notched corners, scanlines, whatever your sci-fi is), and what the UI is "made of" in the fiction (a ship's console, a visor HUD, a paper terminal).
2. Motion rules, not just looks: how things enter (slide, flicker, boot-up), how long a transition takes, and that every screen uses the same one. Generic web dashboards mostly feel generic because they fade and pop.
3. Paste that sheet at the top of every request, and say "follow these rules, don't invent new styles". When something feels off, fix the rule, not the screen, so the fix carries to the next one.
4. Build one reference screen first (the title screen is a good one), get it right, then ask for each new screen "in the same style as the title screen". A rough sketch, like the one above, helps a lot for layout.
5. Check the screens side by side, and the moves between them, not one at a time.

replies.author: KamiYui_5555
replies.body: I really like the idea of fixing the rule instead of the screen. Do you have an example of a screen that felt off and the rule you changed to fix it?

replies.author: pippinlitli
replies.body:
Yes. The screen that felt off was the first play screen of a small asteroid-dodge game I made. It started the moment the page loaded, so the round was already running while you were still reading the controls, and you could hit game over before you'd pressed a key. It felt like a demo that was already in motion, not a game waiting for you.

The rule I changed was not the look of that screen. It was: nothing in the world moves until the player has pressed a key or a button on a start screen. I reused that same idea when I added a pause later: P or a pause button stops everything, a "Paused" message stays on screen, and nothing resumes until you press again. I didn't restyle the game-over or pause overlays one by one; I fixed the "wait for the player" rule, and the later screen followed it.
